newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: U.S. Jews to press Swiss banks on shredded files.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Jews to press Swiss banks on shredded files.

text.p: American Jewish leaders due to meet top Swiss bankers on Friday said they would stress that the destruction of Holocaust-era records by Union Bank of Switzerland (UBS) was "intolerable".

The U.S. Anti-Defamation League (ADL) also urged Swiss politicians and banks to treat a security guard who discovered the shredding as a hero for rescuing some documents and making the incident public.

"I would have thought that from the highest levels of this country, one would have heard a voice of outrage (at the shredding)," ADL national director Abraham Foxman told a news conference after his group met Berne politicians, including Foreign Minister Flavio Cotti.
"I don't hear the voices of outrage, I hear excuses, and I don't see the celebration of this security guard as a hero," he said.
UBS, which has called the document destruction a "regrettable accident", said it had suspended its head of historical archives, vice-president Erwin Haggenmueller, for ordering the shredding.

UBS, the country's biggest bank, said suspension was routine when employees came under investigation by prosecutors, who are looking at whether the act broke a law protecting bank records during a national hunt for lost accounts left by Holocuast victims.
Prosecutors said some of the documents rescued by the security guard stemmed from the 1930s and 1940s.
"The shredding of documents is not only illegal but intolerable and the banks must take steps to prevent this kind of thing from happening," the ADL's Foxman said.
"We will raise this issue very, very clearly," he added, referring to talks scheduled on Friday between the ADL leadership and senior executives in Zurich.
The meeting will include the head of the Swiss Bankers Association, Georg Krayer, as well as the biggest three institutes -- UBS, Credit Suisse Group and Swiss Bank Corporation (SBC).
Foxman said he would urge the banks to speak out against the destruction of UBS documents, which UBS says were not relevent to customer accounts.

UBS has said the archivist had ordered the records destroyed after judging them to be unimportant. They came from a Swiss bank, Eidgenoessischen Bank, that was active in Germany and acquired by UBS in 1945.

Foxman declined to say whether prosecutors should drop their probe of the security guard, Christoph Meili, for breaking bank secrecy laws by taking the documents but said he should be embraced by the rest of the country.
"If this had happened in the United States, you probably would see him (Meili) in the White House being thanked by the president for saving the image and the dignity of the country," Fox said.

Swiss Jews appealed to the government to pass a law sparing people like Meili who protect records from legal consequences or losing their jobs. Meili was suspended from his job at a private security firm.

Swiss banks are under scrutiny by a government panel of international historians looking at the Swiss wartime financial role and by a joint commission set up by the banks and world Jewish groups to trace lost Holocaust accounts.
